items.prompt: What is the primary way plants that live deep in caves get the energy they need?

options.label: They absorb light from the cave walls
options.feedback: Cave walls do not emit light; total darkness means no photosynthesis can occur for plants.

options.label: They make food using minerals in the rock
options.feedback: Minerals are nutrients, not an energy source; plants can't turn them into food without light.

options.label: They rely on organic matter washed in from outside
options.feedback: That's right — cave plants and animals often depend on food particles carried in by water or animals from the surface.

options.label: They use heat from the earth to make sugar
options.feedback: Heat is not a usable energy source for making sugar; only light or chemical reactions can power that.

items.ok_line: Cave life depends on food brought from outside.
items.ko_line: No light means no photosynthesis in caves.
items.exp_text: In total darkness, plants cannot photosynthesize, so any plant-like life in caves either dies or must receive organic material from the surface. This food can drift in with groundwater, be dropped by animals that travel in and out, or arrive as waste. The key point is that all cave ecosystems ultimately depend on what enters from the lit world above.

items.prompt: What do bacteria at hydrothermal vents use to make their food instead of sunlight?

options.label: Chemical energy from minerals in the hot water
options.feedback: Exactly — they use energy from chemical reactions, a process called chemosynthesis, to build sugars.

options.label: Heat from the vent itself
options.feedback: Heat alone doesn't drive food-making; it's the dissolved chemicals like hydrogen sulfide that supply the energy.

options.label: Electricity generated by the vent's pressure
options.feedback: There's no electricity involved; the energy comes from chemical bonds in minerals.

options.label: Radioactive decay from deep rocks
options.feedback: Radioactivity isn't used for making food; vent bacteria rely on specific chemical reactions.

items.ok_line: Vent bacteria use chemicals, not light.
items.ko_line: It's chemical energy, not heat or electricity.
items.exp_text: Hydrothermal vent bacteria harness energy by breaking down chemicals like hydrogen sulfide that come out of the vent. This process, called chemosynthesis, lets them build sugars from carbon dioxide. That sugar then feeds the entire vent community, from tube worms to crabs, without any sunlight involved.

items.prompt: What is the main food source for animals living on the deep ocean floor far away from hydrothermal vents?

options.label: Seaweed that grows down there
options.feedback: No plants can grow in the dark depths, so seaweed is not found there.

options.label: Dead organic matter sinking from the surface
options.feedback: That's right — the deep sea floor receives a slow rain of dead plankton, fish remains, and other organic debris from the sunlit waters above.

options.label: Chemosynthetic bacteria living all over the mud
options.feedback: Chemosynthetic bacteria are only abundant near vents; the open floor doesn't have enough chemicals for them.

options.label: Small fish that swim up from below
options.feedback: Fish don't come from below; there's nothing deeper than the floor, and they get energy from what falls down.

items.ok_line: Dead surface matter feeds the deep.
items.ko_line: No plants or vents on most of the floor.
items.exp_text: Most of the deep ocean floor is a cold, dark plain far from any vent. Its inhabitants—worms, sea cucumbers, and small crustaceans—eat the steady drizzle of dead plankton, fecal pellets, and other organic bits that sink from the sunlit surface. This 'marine snow' is their only energy input, making life down there utterly dependent on the surface world.

items.prompt: Why do many cave-dwelling animals have pale or colourless bodies?

options.label: Because pigments are not needed in the dark
options.feedback: Exactly — in permanent darkness, colour pigments offer no camouflage or communication value, so they are lost over generations.

options.label: Because they are sick from lack of food
options.feedback: Paleness here is a genetic adaptation, not a sign of illness; they are healthy but simply lack pigment.

options.label: Because the cave water bleaches their skin
options.feedback: Water doesn't bleach them; it's evolution that removes unnecessary colour.

options.label: Because they are all albino
options.feedback: Albinism is a specific genetic condition; many cave animals are pale without being true albinos—they still have some pigment but very little.

items.ok_line: No light means no need for colour.
items.ko_line: It's evolution, not disease or bleaching.
items.exp_text: In caves, there is no sunlight for anything to see colours by. Over many generations, animals that happen to have less pigment survive just as well as those with normal colouration. Since pigmentation costs energy to produce, individuals with reduced pigment waste less energy, so they thrive and pass on their paler genes. The result is that cave creatures commonly appear white or translucent, not because they are sick, but because colour is simply useless there.

items.prompt: Why do tube worms living at hydrothermal vents have no mouth or gut?

options.label: They are plants and make their own food
options.feedback: They are animals, not plants; they don't photosynthesize.

options.label: They absorb food directly through their skin
options.feedback: They don't absorb food through skin; they rely on internal bacteria.

options.label: Because bacteria inside them make food for them
options.feedback: Correct — tube worms host chemosynthetic bacteria in their bodies, and those bacteria provide all the nutrients the worm needs.

options.label: They are dead and don't need to eat
options.feedback: They are alive but just don't eat in the usual way.

items.ko_line: They don't eat; they host bacteria.
items.exp_text: Giant tube worms at hydrothermal vents have completely lost their mouth, stomach, and intestines. Instead, their bodies are packed with chemosynthetic bacteria that convert vent chemicals into sugars. The worm supplies the bacteria with the raw materials it needs, and in return, the bacteria pass back nutrients to the worm. This symbiotic relationship lets the worm live without ever feeding actively.

items.prompt: Why is the deep open ocean completely dark below a certain depth?

options.label: Because the water is too cold for light
options.feedback: Cold doesn't block light; temperature has nothing to do with darkness.

options.label: Because there are too many fish blocking the light
options.feedback: Fish don't block light; the water itself absorbs it.

options.label: Because the bottom is too far away to reflect light
options.feedback: The bottom doesn't reflect light; the ocean surface is what lets light in, and it gets absorbed along the way.

options.label: Because water absorbs sunlight before it can travel that deep
options.feedback: Correct — water molecules absorb light quickly, so after a few hundred meters, no sunlight remains.

items.exp_text: Sunlight enters the ocean from above, but water absorbs it rapidly. Within a few hundred meters, the blue light that penetrates deepest is gone, leaving complete darkness. The depth at which this happens varies but is well above most of the ocean floor, so the vast majority of the deep sea is pitch black.

items.prompt: What do many blind cave fish use to sense their surroundings and find food?

options.label: Their highly developed eyes
options.feedback: Their eyes are reduced or absent; they cannot rely on sight.

options.label: A sensitive lateral line that detects water movements
options.feedback: That's right — the lateral line senses vibrations and pressure changes in the water, letting them 'feel' obstacles and prey.

options.label: Sonar like bats
options.feedback: Bats use echolocation, but cave fish do not; they use the lateral line and smell, not sound echoes.

options.label: Electromagnetic fields from the earth
options.feedback: Cave fish don't detect magnetic fields for navigation; they rely on touch, smell, and water movement.

items.exp_text: Blind cave fish have lost useful eyes, but they compensate with an extremely sensitive lateral line—a row of sensory cells running along their sides. This line detects the tiny water movements caused by swimming prey or nearby rocks, giving them a detailed 'picture' of their surroundings without seeing. Combined with a keen sense of smell, they can find food and avoid collisions in total darkness.

items.prompt: How do the animals that live around a hydrothermal vent get their energy if there is no sunlight?

options.label: From the chemical energy in vent fluids, which their bacteria convert to food
options.feedback: Correct — chemosynthetic bacteria use dissolved chemicals like hydrogen sulfide to make organic matter, and the animals eat those bacteria or the things that do.

options.label: From stored fat that they made while living near the surface
options.feedback: Vent animals don't migrate from the surface; they are permanent residents and rely on vent chemistry.

options.label: From the heat of the vent, which they absorb to stay warm and active
options.feedback: Heat doesn't provide energy to make food; it only warms, which is not enough to sustain life.

options.label: From light produced by glowing rocks
options.feedback: No rocks glow at vents; some animals make their own light, but that's for communication, not energy.

items.ok_line: Chemicals feed the vent food chain.
items.ko_line: It's chemical, not heat or food storage.
items.exp_text: Hydrothermal vents release hot water rich in minerals like hydrogen sulfide. Bacteria extract energy from these chemicals to build sugars, a process called chemosynthesis. These bacteria form the base of the vent food web, being eaten by tiny animals, which in turn are eaten by larger ones like crabs and fish. Thus, the entire community thrives on chemical energy from the Earth's interior, not on sunlight.

items.prompt: Why can life at a hydrothermal vent thrive without ever depending on the sun?

options.label: Because the vent produces its own light for photosynthesis
options.feedback: Vents do not produce usable light for photosynthesis; they emit only faint heat and some light from minerals, not enough for plants.

options.label: Because the vent is so hot that it creates energy directly
options.feedback: Heat is not energy for living things; organisms need chemical or solar energy, not just warmth.

options.label: Because its bacteria get energy from chemicals in the vent water
options.feedback: Exactly — chemosynthesis uses chemical reactions, independent of sunlight, so the whole food chain can run without any solar input.

options.label: Because the vent animals eat each other endlessly without needing new energy
options.feedback: Eating each other just transfers energy; it doesn't create it—new energy must come from somewhere, and that's the chemicals.

items.ko_line: It's chemosynthesis, not heat or light.
items.exp_text: At hydrothermal vents, the base of the food web is chemosynthetic bacteria that use the energy released from chemical reactions, such as oxidizing hydrogen sulfide. This process doesn't require light or photosynthesis, so it works in the dark depths. Because these bacteria produce food, everything else—worms, crabs, and fish—can survive there even though no sunlight ever reaches them. Thus, the vent ecosystem is completely independent of solar energy.
